known_trends.name: Climate change and adaptation
known_trends.statement: Extreme and compound weather grows more frequent and costly, so adapting infrastructure, health systems, settlements and livelihoods becomes routine work for governments, businesses and communities.

known_trends.name: The net zero transformation
known_trends.statement: Economies decarbonise towards net zero: clean energy, electrification and low-emission industries grow, while demand for some traditional exports declines and new markets emerge.

known_trends.name: Resource scarcity and efficiency
known_trends.statement: Demand for food, water, energy and minerals strains supply, so efficiency, recycling, substitutes and the competition for critical resources all intensify.

known_trends.name: Biodiversity loss and environmental degradation
known_trends.statement: Ecosystems and biodiversity keep declining, and protecting and restoring them becomes a policy and investment priority alongside emissions.

known_trends.name: Population ageing
known_trends.statement: People live longer and fertility stays low, so populations age: many more people over 65 and 85, with lasting economic and fiscal pressure.

known_trends.name: Rising demand for health, care and support
known_trends.statement: Ageing, chronic and emerging diseases and rising expectations lift demand for health, care and support services, which grow as a share of the economy and the workforce.

known_trends.name: Geopolitical competition and fragmentation
known_trends.statement: Strategic competition between powers grows, trade and investment fragment along security lines, and governments work harder to secure stability, supply and growth.

known_trends.name: Economic weight shifting east and south
known_trends.statement: The economic and political influence of Asia and the global south keeps growing relative to Europe and North America.

known_trends.name: A changing security paradigm
known_trends.statement: Security threats widen beyond conventional military ones, and defence and security spending and planning change with them.

known_trends.name: The digital and data economy
known_trends.statement: Digitisation of services, commerce, work and government keeps accelerating, and data becomes a core asset of organisations and economies.

known_trends.name: Artificial intelligence and autonomous systems
known_trends.statement: Artificial intelligence and autonomous systems spread across industries, raising productivity and changing which tasks people do.

known_trends.name: The changing nature of work
known_trends.statement: Work changes in form and content: new skills are in demand, employment becomes more varied, and technology reshapes jobs.

known_trends.name: Diversifying education and learning
known_trends.statement: Education and training diversify in form, provider and timing, towards learning throughout working life.

known_trends.name: Diversifying inequalities
known_trends.statement: Inequalities of income, wealth and opportunity persist and take new forms, within and between countries.

known_trends.name: Diversity, equity and transparency in decisions
known_trends.statement: Diversity, equity and transparency matter more in business, policy and community decisions, and trust depends on them.

known_trends.name: Continuing urbanisation
known_trends.statement: More of the world's people live in cities, which concentrates demand for housing, infrastructure and services.

known_trends.name: Growing consumerism
known_trends.statement: Consumption keeps growing with a rising global middle class, with consequences for resources, waste and markets.

known_trends.name: The increasing significance of migration
known_trends.statement: Migration grows in scale and political salience, shaping labour markets, skills and societies.

known_trends.name: The increasing influence of new governing systems
known_trends.statement: Governance shifts beyond the nation state: networks, platforms, cities and other non-state actors gain influence over rules and decisions.

known_trends.name: Indigenous knowledge, data sovereignty and cultural and intellectual property
known_trends.statement: Research and policy are expected to protect and elevate Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander knowledge systems, with First Nations people leading research that affects them, and with traditional knowledge, language, data sovereignty, cultural expressions and other intellectual property respected and protected.

known_trends.name: Espionage, foreign interference and cyber threats to critical systems
known_trends.statement: Espionage and foreign interference run at very high levels, and state and non-state actors grow more willing and able to intrude on networks and disrupt critical infrastructure, so the security of systems, data and research becomes a standing concern for every organisation that holds them.

known_trends.name: Mis- and disinformation and the contest for trust
known_trends.statement: Misinformation, disinformation and polarisation test trust in democratic institutions, and governments and researchers look for ways to strengthen that trust and people's ability to judge information.

known_trends.name: Rearmament and a sovereign defence industrial base
known_trends.statement: Defence spending rises worldwide and in Australia, and governments build domestic capacity to make, sustain and rapidly adapt military equipment, munitions and dual-use technology, with allies sharing advanced technology under arrangements such as AUKUS.

known_trends.name: The return of industrial policy
known_trends.statement: Governments use funds, tax incentives and guarantees to build strategic industries at home (clean energy, green metals, low-emission fuels, critical minerals and defence), under banners such as Future Made in Australia.

pathways.P1: This development could change how many patents, trade marks, designs or plant breeder's rights are sought in Australia, of what kinds, or by whom.
pathways.P2: This development could make IP rights more or less valuable to Australian businesses and creators, against substitutes such as speed, secrecy, open models or control of data and platforms.
pathways.P3: This development could change how IP rights are examined, granted, administered or enforced.
pathways.P4: This development could affect public trust in, or the perceived fairness of, the IP system.
pathways.P5: This development could affect IP Australia's fee income, workforce, technology, security or mandate.
pathways.P6: This development could change Australia's ability to benefit from new ideas: their commercialisation, their use and their contribution to productivity.

sources.coverage: The data collections CSIRO publishes on its Data Access Portal (DAP): research datasets, models and software, each listed under the ANZSRC 2020 fields of research (divisions) it is filed under. One source reads the portal's search feed once per division (22 feeds; the owner's request, 2026-10-15), newest first, 100 a feed; an item filed under several divisions is one record carrying each division in its `topics`. About 140 new collections a month across the divisions (2026-09-15 to 10-14, up to 12 a day); busy divisions fill their 100 in about five months (environmental sciences: 2026-04-30 to 10-08), small ones hold years (philosophy: 1 collection). Law and legal studies, the 23rd division, has no collections (2026-10-15) and is left out. Titles, links, dates, divisions and descriptions (D-024). CSIRO's research publications (publications.csiro.au) are a gap (D-023, D-024).
sources.history_start: each feed reaches back 100 collections: months for busy divisions, years for small ones
known_biases: CSIRO's own research only, and only what it chooses to deposit; strongest in environmental, earth, agricultural and physical sciences

Version updates of a collection may appear as new items
sources.licence: Each collection's data carry their own licence (CC BY 4.0 by default under CSIRO's deposit terms); no licence for the portal's metadata was found, and csiro.au states CSIRO copyright without an open licence (2026-10-15, read through search results: CSIRO's sites refuse the build session). territories.aim: Uncover how we can strengthen the protection and enforcement of IP.
territories.description: How Australian rights holders, especially small businesses, protect and enforce their intellectual property at home and overseas: infringement, counterfeiting, piracy, scams and disputes, and the agencies, platforms and services that help or fail them, including the cost and stress of enforcement.
territories.name: Protect Australian IP

territories.aim: Equip stakeholders with more ways to use the IP system.
territories.description: How innovators, especially small businesses and those under-served today, work out what is worth protecting and obtain suitable rights with confidence: awareness, cost, timing, complexity, AI and digital tools that simplify identification and application, and protection that fits iterative, collaborative development.
territories.name: Empower others

territories.aim: Meaningfully extend the utility and value of IP.
territories.description: How businesses understand, demonstrate and use the commercial value of their intellectual property: valuation, IP-backed investment and finance, licensing and partnerships, commercialisation and growth, platforms that link registered rights to commercial services, and government priorities for manufacturing, critical minerals and emerging technology.
territories.name: Amplify Australian IP

territories.aim: Work in new ways with ecosystem actors.
territories.description: How businesses reach IP support through organisations they already trust, and how partnerships extend an IP office's reach: attorneys, legal and IP service providers, advisers, accelerators, industry bodies, platforms and other government services, and the gaps between them.
territories.name: Cultivate our ecosystem

territories.aim: Reconsider our raison d'etre in light of a changing world.
territories.description: Whether the purpose and role of an IP office should change: generative AI and inventorship, ownership and value; Indigenous knowledge and geographical indications; IP used to solve societal problems; protection that enables sharing and access; access as a right; government using IP to shape incentives; and the reach of post-registration responsibilities.
territories.name: Revisit our purpose
